newsitem.title: USA: Key U.S. lawmakers sponsor bill on China WTO entry.
newsitem.headline: Key U.S. lawmakers sponsor bill on China WTO entry.

text.p: Citing what they called an unsustainable trade gap with China, key House Democrats Thursday introduced legislation requiring a Congressional vote on U.S. approval of Beijing's bid to join the World Trade Organisation.

House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt, D-Mo., who, along with Representative David Bonior, the second ranking Democrat in the House, and Representative Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., introduced the legislation, said the bill so far had 40 backers and he expected more support from both Democrats and Republicans who control both houses of Congress.
The legislation is being introduced at a time of mounting public attention on allegations that China tried to funnel money into U.S. election campaigns.

Gephardt told reporters at a news conference he thought lawmakers would be more influenced by the ballooning trade deficit with China and Beijing's human rights record than by the unfolding campaign finance scandal.
"I don't think all of these other stories will have a big impact one way or another," Gephardt said.

But Pelosi said the campaign finance scandal "sheds a brighter light" on China and was encouraging Americans to pay closer attention to other issues involving U.S.-Sino relations. Pelosi, an outspoken critic of China's human rights record, was one of the lawmakers warned by Federal Bureau of Investigation agents that China was trying to funnel money into U.S. election campaigns to influence U.S. officials.
"As with anything, when it is in the news there is more attention paid," she said.
China has strongly denied the reports.

The legislation is the same as that supported last year by Gephardt, who is a potential rival to Vice President Al Gore for the Democratic presidential nomination in the 2000 election campaign. The White House has argued against the proposed legislation, saying it was not needed because of ongoing consultations with Congress.
Representative Doug Bereuter, R-Neb., chairman of the House Asia and Pacific subcommittee, said the proposed legislation would harm U.S. commercial interests and foreign policy.
In a statement he said the legislation could force the Chinese to walk away from the negotiating table.

But the three sponsors said at a news conference that the bill ensures Congress' constitutional authority over international commerce in the case of China's entry into the WTO. Gephardt said the law would help Congress "ensure that we get the best deal possible by becoming a real partner in negotiations with the Administration. It is important for China to understand the seriousness with which we view this issue."
The three argued that China's economy was too big, and the trade gap with the United States too large, to allow a long transition period for Beijing's entry into the WTO.

"China should become a member of the WTO, but under the right commercial conditions," Pelosi said. "The future of our economy is at stake. The current U.S.-China trade relationship from the standpoint of our future economic health is unsustainable."

The U.S. Commerce Department reported on Thursday that the U.S. trade deficit with China jumped sharply by 40.8 percent in January to $3.72 billion from $2.65 billion in December. The overall U.S. deficit with China has risen rapidly in recent years, hitting $40 billion last year. It is second only to the U.S. trade deficit with Japan.
